candidate.title: Download the Utilization of Sick Call in New York City Jails Report
candidate.summary: The New York City Board of Correction has completed an in-depth analysis of the sick call process within NYC jails for calendar year 2023. This report evaluates how well current systems, including both the Department of Correction's (DOC) sick call process and Correctional Health Services' (CHS) Health Triage Line, meet the medical needs of people in custody. Key findings reveal that over a third of sick call requests resulted in people in custody not being escorted to their appointments, and less than half of those who were escorted were seen within the mandated timeframe of one business day. The Board recognizes the distinction between the CHS Health Triage Line and the DOC's sick call process, while also affirming that both mechanisms function to address non-emergency health concerns, as per the Board's Minimum Standards. The analysis in this report reflects both methods of accessing care and highlights areas for improvement in coordination between the two systems. To address these issues, the Board has proposed several recommendations, including the re-establishment of a DOC-led sick call process, the development of a real-time scheduling dashboard, and improved tracking of healthcare encounters. The goal is to enhance the timeliness and effectiveness of medical care provided to people in custody, aiming for at least a 95% compliance rate within the next six months. The report also suggests implementing patient satisfaction surveys to further refine the process. candidate.summary: The State of Workers’ Rights in New York City DCA's Office of Labor Policy & Standards (OLPS) released a report “The State of Workers’ Rights in New York City,” which details emerging gaps in labor protections and offers policy solutions to these growing concerns. The report summarizes the testimony of 110 workers given during a public hearing in April 2017 that was convened by DCA, in collaboration with the New York City Commission on Human Rights and the Mayor’s Office of Immigrant Affairs (MOIA). Through their testimony, workers articulated the many challenges and concerns facing immigrant, paid care, and contingent workers. Their personal narratives reveal a pattern of egregious workplace violations affecting a diverse range of industries, demonstrating that wage theft, harassment, and discrimination are not limited to low-wage industries, but increasingly pose threats in traditionally higher-paying jobs as well, including writers and academics. candidate.summary: Working in NYC: Results from the 2017 Empire State Poll In early 2017, DCA's Office of Labor Policy & Standards (OLPS) and the Worker Institute at Cornell partnered to add a series of questions to the Empire State Poll, a representative phone survey of 800 New York State residents conducted annually by the Cornell Survey Research Institute. The survey questions developed by OLPS and the Worker Institute addressed a range of issues related to inequality, working conditions, and the role of city and local government in protecting immigrants and defending worker rights.
